draft.title: Collectivisation
card: Collectivisation was the Soviet policy of merging peasants' small private farms into large state-controlled collective farms. It began in 1929, and the state pushed it hard from the winter of 1929 to 1930.
Stalin wanted grain to feed the growing cities and to sell abroad. That money was to help pay for industrial growth. He also wanted tighter party control over the countryside.
Many peasants resisted. Some killed their livestock rather than hand it over. The state targeted better-off peasants, called kulaks, and deported or imprisoned many of them.
The state seized grain, often leaving villages short of food. Famine followed in 1932 to 1933 and killed millions, especially in Ukraine and Kazakhstan.
draft.remember: Collectivisation put farming under state control to supply grain for industry, and the cost was resistance, seizures and famine.

a.q: Why did Stalin's government pursue collectivisation?
opts: To get grain for cities and export, and tighten control
To give peasants full ownership of the land they farmed
To end the state's need to collect grain from farms
To reward kulaks for producing surplus food
a.why: The state wanted grain to feed workers and to sell abroad, and it wanted more control over peasants. Giving peasants ownership is wrong because collectivisation took farms out of private hands.
a.clue: Think about who needed the grain and who held the power.

b.q: In 1930 a village in Ukraine kills its cattle rather than give them to a new collective farm. What does this action best show?
opts: Peasant resistance to collectivisation
Support for the state's grain targets
A planned result of the Five-Year Plans
The success of the campaign against kulaks
b.why: Killing livestock to keep it from the state was a common way peasants resisted. It does not show support for the policy. It also made food shortages worse, as it reduced the animals available.
b.clue: Ask whether the villagers wanted to hand over their animals.

a.best: To get grain for cities and export, and tighten control

problems.detail: The card dates the famine to 1932 to 1933 for both Ukraine and Kazakhstan. The Kazakh famine began earlier, around 1930 to 1931, and lasted to 1933. Consider saying 'Famine followed, worst in 1932 to 1933' or giving Kazakhstan its own dates.
